subject: Agriculture
title: Mycotoxins and Food Safety
description: Learn Mycotoxins and Food Safety in one minute.

hook.text: Aflatoxin, produced by a common grain mold, is one of the most potent carcinogens known. It contaminates 25% of crops.

buildup.text: Aspergillus fungi grow on corn, peanuts, and tree nuts—especially in warm, humid storage conditions.

discovery.text: Chronic low-dose aflatoxin exposure causes liver cancer. In developing countries, it kills 30,000 people annually.

twist.text: Rich countries test and reject contaminated grain. Poor countries eat it because they can't afford to throw food away.

climax.text: Biocontrol fungi—harmless Aspergillus strains that outcompete toxin producers—are showing promise in Africa.

punchline.text: The mold is invisible. The cancer takes decades. The poorest pay the price.

quiz.question: What health effect does chronic aflatoxin exposure cause?

details.summary: Mycotoxins are toxic compounds produced by fungi that contaminate grain, nuts, and other crops before and after harvest. This topic covers major mycotoxins like aflatoxin, their health effects, and the global challenge of keeping food supplies safe from fungal contamination.
details.whyItMatters: Aflatoxin alone contaminates 25% of the world's food crops and causes liver cancer. In developing countries, mycotoxin exposure is chronic and contributes to stunted growth in children and immune suppression.
takeaways: Mycotoxins are toxic fungal metabolites that contaminate 25% of global food crops
Aflatoxin is a potent carcinogen produced by Aspergillus fungi on grain and nuts
Proper drying, storage, and monitoring are essential to prevent mycotoxin buildup

faq.question: What are the most dangerous mycotoxins in the food supply?
faq.answer: Aflatoxins (from Aspergillus fungi) cause liver cancer and are the most potent natural carcinogens known. Fumonisins contaminate maize and are linked to esophageal cancer. Deoxynivalenol from Fusarium causes nausea and immune suppression in grain consumers.

faq.question: How can mycotoxin contamination in food be prevented?
faq.answer: Key prevention strategies include rapid post-harvest drying to below 13% moisture, proper ventilated storage, crop rotation to reduce Fusarium buildup, breeding resistant varieties, and regular testing of grain lots. Biocontrol using non-toxic Aspergillus strains is also emerging.
